data.title: RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra urges banks to step up lending to small, micro enterprises for greater economic gains
data.description:
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra on Saturday urged banks to focus more on lending to small businesses, saying the broader economic benefits of such lending are significantly greater.

PTI reported that while speaking at a financial inclusion camp organised by Bank of Maharashtra at Waksai village in Mawal taluka, Pune district, Malhotra said a Rs 1,000-crore loan to a large business enterprise would benefit only one individual or business.

“However, if we provide the same amount to small enterprises, the overall impact and benefits could be at least a hundred times greater,” Malhotra said. He added that the impact could be a thousand times greater if the amount were distributed among micro-enterprise borrowers.

The career bureaucrat-turned-central banker said this was a “special appeal”, based on the gains he had witnessed among a wider section of people as banks increased their focus on rural areas and economically weaker segments.

“We must remember that development should be inclusive. When we talk about development, it must be development for everyone. It is important that we take all sections of society and all regions along with us,” he added.

Referring to the government's financial inclusion initiative, under which more than 60 crore bank accounts have been opened, Malhotra said the focus must now extend to financial and digital literacy.

Banking services are increasingly being accessed through digital platforms, he said, underlining the importance of exercising caution while using digital banking services.

He also cautioned people against fraudulent financial schemes targeting unsuspecting investors.

“If someone approaches you with an offer promising returns of 20%, 30% or even 40% over a short period, you should be extremely cautious. Such unusually high returns are often associated with hidden risks or fraudulent schemes,” he said.

Malhotra urged people never to share their one-time passwords (OTPs) and to be careful about clicking on unknown links or responding to suspicious messages.

“I would strongly encourage all of you to adopt digital banking services, but do so responsibly and with complete awareness. We must ensure that people are protected from all kinds of digital fraud,” he said.

The camp, which saw a turnout of more than 500 people, aims to bring essential banking services and government-backed social security schemes closer to the community. Malhotra said such camps would be held across the country until December 31.

Bank of Maharashtra Managing Director and Chief Executive Nidhu Saxena and other banking sector officials also attended the camp, which is part of the Department of Financial Services' (DFS) nationwide Financial Inclusion Saturation Campaign.

Saxena said the bank had expanded its business correspondent network to 10,000 from 3,000 two years ago. It has conducted 3,691 camps so far, including those organised by the regional rural bank it sponsors.

(With PTI inputs)

data.title: Micron and Sandisk stocks might look like bargains, but analysts say that's actually a red flag
data.description:
By Hannah Pedone

Cheap valuation multiples for memory stocks have historically been associated with peak pricing levels, according to analysts

Shares of Micron fell nearly 14% on Friday.

Memory stocks were among the biggest decliners as the technology sector bled red ink on Friday.

Shares of Micron Technology (MU) closed down 14% on Friday, while shares of Sandisk (SNDK) fell 16%. Western Digital's stock (WDC) sank 12%.

The pressure on these stocks is mounting. Micron shares are down 50.99% from their peak, while Sandisk shares are down 72.85% from their highs and Western Digital's stock has shed 64.97%.

The chip sector in general has been hit hard due to various factors. Those include concerns that politicians could get stricter about data-center construction, leadership uncertainty at Nvidia (NVDA) and the idea that Anthropic's (ANT) IPO might have sucked attention away from the broader tech sector.

Then there is the perennial debate over the price-to-earnings multiples of memory stocks.

Micron and Sandisk shares both trade at meaningful discounts to their recent historical valuations. Micron's stock trades at 3.76 times estimated earnings for the next 12 months, versus a two-year average of 9.10 times. Sandisk's multiple of 3.04 times forward earnings expectations is below its 10.47-times average since the time of its separation from Western Digital in February 2025.

But Brendan Burke, the research director for semiconductors, supply chain and emerging tech at the Futurum Group, says that low price-to-earnings ratios for memory stocks are a "warning label, not a bargain sign."

"Investors have learned over decades to sell memory stocks at peak earnings, because the earnings side of that ratio has historically collapsed when the cycle turns," he said.

"A multiple in the low single digits tells you the market is pricing today's profits as a peak," he added.

Admittedly, there are some caveats. The historical precedent "ignores that AI has changed the shape of this cycle." Some types of memory, like high-bandwidth memory and solid-state-drive storage, are tied to what he called "mission-critical data-center buildouts," as opposed to memory for PCs and handsets. That distinction means the earnings might be "more durable than these multiples imply," Burke said.

William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji told MarketWatch that there's a limit to the usefulness of low P/E ratios as a "valuation support metric."

Memory stocks often see "extreme volatility in pricing," CreditSights analyst Andy Li added, and that can lead to boom-and-bust cycles.

If investors assume the market is still cyclical, a "dramatic price decline may well be in the cards," he said. "The price action reflects that fear."

Li explained that cyclical stocks like memory often top with "very low" price-to-earnings multiples, because that's when their estimated earnings for the next 12 months are "most inflated." Meanwhile, they also bottom with relatively high multiples, following the same logic, he said.

Separately, he added that the fact that monthly options expire on Friday could also be a technical factor affecting the stocks.

-Hannah Pedone

data.title: Hero MotoCorp gets ITAT relief on ₹27 crore tax demand for six assessment years

Hero MotoCorp Ltd. has received relief from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) in connection with an outstanding tax demand of approximately ₹27 crore.

That's for six assessment years from 2013-14 to 2017-18 and 2019-20.

In a regulatory filing, the company said it downloaded an appeal order dated November 20, 2026, from the ITAT portal on the same day.

The order grants relief to Hero MotoCorp in respect of the outstanding tax demand of approximately ₹27 crore.

The company had earlier informed the stock exchanges about the assessment orders and demand notices received from the Income Tax Department for the six assessment years through communications dated April 4, 2024, May 25, 2024 and March 12, 2026.

These updates also covered subsequent rectification and reduction of the demands.

Shares of the company closed at ₹5,536 apiece on the NSE on Friday, November 20.

data.title: Chainflip’s FLIP drops 34% after attacker drains $4.86 million from vault with suspected key compromise
data.description:
Cross-chain decentralized exchange Chainflip (FLIP) paused its protocol on Saturday morning after security firms detected an attack which looted about $4.86 million in ETH and stablecoins from its Ethereum-based vault, apparently using a valid signature from the protocol's own signing key.

"We're aware of a potential exploit affecting Chainflip vaults," the protocol shared on X. "As a precaution, the protocol is being put into full safe mode. Deposits, withdrawals, swaps and quoting are disabled."

Chainflip's FLIP token plummeted about 34% following the 2:10 a.m. ET exploit, per The Block's Chainflip price page. The token's market capitalization dropped from about $41.6 million to $27.1 million as of publication time.

Entire attack took under 10 minutes

Security firm Decurity first shared details of the attack on X through its Defimon Alerts bot. The alert noted Chainflip's Ethereum vault was drained of "its entire liquid balance," making up 520.2 ETH, 3.25M USDC and 758K USDT worth around $4.86 million at the time. The alert said that rather than exploiting a smart contract bug, the attacker apparently obtained access to the validator network's aggregate signing key, meaning the secret code that authorizes transfers.

The attacker launched the hack through a fresh wallet, and later sent nearly all the proceeds through mixing protocol Tornado Cash, per security firm AMLBot. "The laundering was executed with high-speed automation," AMLBot stated, noting that the stablecoins moved too fast for USDC issuer Circle and USDT issuer Tether to freeze the tokens, as the whole attack took place in under 10 minutes.

Chainflip has not said how the attacker may have compromised the key, which is jointly controlled by the protocol's 150 validators and rotated every three days; the last rotation happened on Nov. 18 at 4:53 p.m. ET, about two and a half days before the exploit. No one validator is supposed to have access to the full key; rather, each holds a piece and 100 out of 150 are required to sign transactions.

Blockchain data firm Bitquery noted in its investigation that Chainflip's key changed about an hour and 45 minutes after the theft. The timing suggests Chainflip rotated the compromised key to prevent further thefts, though Bitquery noted that no conclusions can be drawn from timing alone.

In another quirk Bitquery noted, the attacker's transaction carried a strange nonce, or a unique number that every Chainflip withdrawal is stamped with. That number, each of which is only used once, usually increments by one to prevent anyone from replaying old transactions, but rather than having a nonce around 315,000 like other transactions around that time, the attacker's nonce was a 39-digit number.

That suggests the approval wasn't made through Chainflip's normal system, which would have handed out the next number on the counter, but that the attacker somehow produced a valid signature outside that system. Bitquery noted that the drain was the only one of 299,677 signatures since 2023 that broke the count.

Chainflip's vaults on other chains like Bitcoin and Solana were apparently unaffected by the attack. However, a transaction on the Bitcoin network moved the nearly 10.5 BTC from a previous Chainflip vault address to a brand new address about two hours after Chainflip paused the protocol, suggesting another way the protocol is safeguarding its remaining funds, though its purpose has not been confirmed. That transaction has not yet been reported by security firms.

Chainflip previously repaid victims of Tron exploit

Chainflip previously suffered an exploit on Sept. 12 that saw an attacker abuse a flaw in how Chainflip processed Tron transaction memos to double-process six withdrawals on the Tron network.

The protocol's validators later voted to reimburse the affected liquidity providers (LPs) using the protocol's "surplus funds," which Chainflip described as "a combination of many things. It is both excess funds held by the protocol through gas fee interactions, assets sent to Chainflip in error that the protocol could not automatically return, and other sometimes so far unexplained surpluses that have built up in the vaults since launch."

Chainflip has not said whether it plans to reimburse the victims of the current hack. Chainflip did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Block.

This is a developing story.

data.title: VanEck's Matthew Sigel stays bullish on Bitcoin after the midterms
data.description:
Bitcoin is having a rough November. Matthew Sigel is unbothered.

VanEck's head of digital assets research went on CNBC shortly after the US midterms and repeated his bullish case for Bitcoin. He made it as markets fretted over Democratic gains in Congress, a scenario widely labeled a "blue wave." Bitcoin is currently trading around $60,000. By mid-November it was down about 24% from its pre-election high, so his timing took some nerve.

Sigel's argument starts in an unexpected place. He suggested a Democratic-led Congress could help Bitcoin, not hurt it.

His reasoning runs through fiscal policy. On CNBC, Sigel said rising government spending and debt issuance under a Democratic majority could benefit Bitcoin. In his view, that would limit its long-term risk compared with other assets.

Sigel didn't brush off the recent weakness. As of mid-November, Bitcoin had been bouncing between $58,000 and $65,000. He blamed that slide on liquidity tightening and a few other short-term pressures.

One of those pressures came from outside crypto entirely. Sigel cited the Anthropic IPO as a factor weighing on the market.

Sigel leaned on a historical comparison to back his view. He pointed to the 2022 midterms, after which Bitcoin rallied by approximately 300%.

He argued that the setup then resembles the one now. He noted similar Federal Reserve rate conditions and earlier market crises that shaped where Bitcoin went next.

Sigel also pointed to on-chain data, the activity recorded directly on Bitcoin's public ledger. Specifically, he flagged a metric called NUPL, short for net unrealized profit/loss.

Sigel said NUPL currently sits in the "Hope/Fear" zone. His read is that long-term holders are not capitulating, even as liquidity dries up.

His analysis also draws on Bitcoin's four-year cycle. That pattern loosely tracks the network's halving events, when the reward for mining new coins is cut in half.

Sigel's comments fit with VanEck's broader house view on Bitcoin. The firm has forecast a $100,000 Bitcoin price by 2027, tied to its cycle models.

The firm sees two main catalysts on the road to 2027: institutional adoption and regulatory certainty.

VanEck has skin in the game here. As an asset manager with digital asset products, it benefits when investors grow more comfortable with crypto.

The on-chain signals are worth watching closely. If NUPL slides from "Hope/Fear" into capitulation territory, Sigel's claim that long-term holders are holding firm would come under pressure. A move back toward the top of the $58,000 to $65,000 range would support his argument that the selloff was temporary.

VanEck has named regulatory clarity as a key catalyst. How the incoming Congress approaches digital asset rules could shape whether the 2027 target looks prescient or optimistic.

data.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ on U.S. firms building data centers abroad
data.description:
President Donald Trump has said that his administration will ban U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries, and those who do so will face a “tremendous tax,” a policy move that caught his own staff members by surprise.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said during a press conference at the White House on Friday after returning from his trip to Asia. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story,” Trump added. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now they’re here.”

His remarks came after public backlash against data centers fueled victories for some of the Democratic candidates who pledged tougher regulations on their construction in states such as Texas in the lead-up to the U.S. midterm elections.

The massive warehouse-style buildings incorporating numerous computer chips are crucial to the AI boom, as they help run popular large language models such as Claude and ChatGPT. The U.S. is home to about 3,000 data centers, while another 1,500 structures are in various stages of development as of April, according to the Pew Research Center.

“We’re going to fight very hard for the data centers,” Trump said, noting that "we're going to keep it all in this country.”

If implemented, Trump's policy will be a major headwind for AI hyperscalers such as Meta and Alphabet , which have signed agreements worth billions of dollars to build overseas data centers as part of business and regulatory requirements.

“We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they’re great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They’re tremendous assets,” Trump said.

The Board of Directors of Nanologica AB (publ) (“Nanologica” or the “Company”) has today, pursuant to the authorisation granted by the Annual General Meeting on 21 May 2026, resolved on a directed issue of 1,590,747 units, corresponding to 15,907,470 shares, to certain guarantors in the Company’s recently completed rights issue (the “Rights Issue”), in accordance with the previously announced guarantee agreements (the “Compensation Issue”). The subscription price in the Compensation Issue is SEK 1.68 per unit, corresponding to SEK 0.168 per share. Payment will be made by setting off the guarantors’ claims for guarantee compensation against the subscription amount.

Background

On 19 November 2026, Nanologica announced the outcome of the Rights Issue, for which the subscription period ended on 17 November 2026. Following the utilisation of guarantee commitments, the Rights Issue was subscribed to approximately 77.55 percent and will provide the Company with approximately SEK 85.7 million before deduction of issue costs and set-off of claims.

Guarantee compensation and the Compensation Issue

As previously announced, Ardena is entitled to guarantee compensation of 14 percent of the guaranteed amount in the form of newly issued units. For Bergs Securities AB’s bottom guarantee commitment, compensation is payable in cash at 10 percent of the guaranteed amount or, at Bergs Securities AB’s option, in the form of newly issued units at 14 percent of the guaranteed amount. Bergs Securities AB has elected to receive all of its guarantee compensation in the form of newly issued units.

The Compensation Issue comprises a total of 1,590,747 units, corresponding to 15,907,470 shares. The subscription price is SEK 1.68 per unit, corresponding to SEK 0.168 per share, which is the same as the subscription price in the Rights Issue. Payment will be made in full by setting off the guarantors’ claims for guarantee compensation against the subscription amount. Accordingly, the Company will receive no cash proceeds from the Compensation Issue.

The Compensation Issue does not include the guarantee compensation payable to T&M Participation AB, through which the Chairman of the Board, Thomas Eldered, provided a top guarantee commitment. A proposal concerning the guarantee compensation payable to T&M Participation AB has been submitted for approval at the Extraordinary General Meeting on 30 November 2026. No compensation is payable for Sterling Pharma Solutions’ top guarantee commitment.

Reasons for deviating from shareholders’ preferential rights

The reason for deviating from shareholders’ preferential rights is to fulfil the Company’s obligations to Bergs Securities AB and Ardena Gent NV under the previously announced guarantee agreements. The Compensation Issue enables the guarantors to set off their claims for guarantee compensation against the subscription amount for the newly issued units. The Board of Directors considers that settling the guarantee compensation in units rather than cash benefits the Company’s financial position and is in the interests of its shareholders, as it preserves the Company’s cash resources.

Number of shares, share capital and dilution

The Compensation Issue will increase the number of shares in Nanologica by 15,907,470 and the share capital by SEK 318,149.40. Following the Rights Issue and the Compensation Issue, the Company will have 854,571,322 shares and a share capital of SEK 17,091,426.44. The Compensation Issue will result in dilution of approximately 1.86 percent of the shares and votes in the Company, calculated by dividing the number of new shares issued in the Compensation Issue by the total number of shares outstanding following the Rights Issue and the Compensation Issue.

Nanologica has engaged Redeye AB, Bergs Securities AB and Navia Corporate Finance AB as Joint Bookrunners, and Advokatfirman Lindahl KB as legal adviser in connection with the Rights Issue. Bergs Securities AB is also acting as issuing agent in connection with the Rights Issue.

data.title: After a Lifetime of Looking Ahead, a Chance to Look Back and Give Thanks — WSJ
data.description:
By Stephen Kreider Yoder and Karen Kreider Yoder

Retirement Rookies

The first few years in retirement are often the most difficult. But they also can set the stage for how you'll fill the years ahead — both financially and psychologically. Stephen Kreider Yoder, 69, a longtime Wall Street Journal editor, joined his wife, Karen Kreider Yoder, 70, in retirement in late 2022. In this monthly Retirement Rookies column, the Yoders chronicle some of the issues they are dealing with early in retirement.

Steve

I am writing these words filled with gratitude.

As Thanksgiving nears, Karen and I have found that retirement is an especially good time to take stock — a rare chance to look back, to appreciate the relationships that endured, the health that still allows us to enjoy our days, and the simple gift of having time that is finally our own.

We are grateful for 5 a.m. on Monday mornings, when one of us brews coffee and plucks the San Francisco Chronicle off the stoop, the other rolls back over to sleep, and neither has a job to break the reverie. It's a daily reminder of just how thankful we are for each other.

We give thanks that we can age in a city that delights us with its row houses, hills, dunes and friends, where caring people urge us to help the unfortunate around us. We are thankful for the road that starts at our front door and sweeps us off on adventures across America.

And we count the blessings that put us here — the privileges we were born into as Americans in loving families, the wide-open career opportunities, the institutions that helped us save for retirement.

Our biggest blessings are the people who got us here. Many of them, I can no longer thank.

I can't thank my expository-writing professor — Mrs. Hartzler, she asked us to call her — a stern master whose glare scared many students. She demanded logic, brevity, grammar and meticulous word choice in a way I found so compelling that I changed my major to English my senior year. She died the year after I graduated, and I see her face every time I edit.

I can't thank Greg, my first boss in the U.S., a curmudgeon who distrusted authority and taught this meek reporter to be tough enough to be his deputy and guided me into my editing career.

I can't thank my late mother, who grew up in a dirt-poor Texas Panhandle farm family and fascinated us with childhood tales. Classmates called her "white trash," she told us with an impish grin, and her first chewing gum was a wad she plucked off a Perryton sidewalk. Her girlhood poverty was a point of pride, and she instilled in me both frugality and the conviction that my potential transcended class.

Fortunately, I can still thank my father, who grew up on a hardscrabble Iowa farm and is still sharp at age 95. In February 1961, he and my mother trundled us children up the gangway onto the SS President Cleveland in San Francisco and shipped off to become career missionaries in Japan — an unimaginable leap of faith to a land still recovering from war.

Their sacrifices in leaving America gave me a wondrous childhood in Northern Japan, where I learned the joys of urban living while straddling cultures. Our family budget was tight, and I concluded that it was my job to find work to fund hobbies and adventures, capitalizing on the independence my parents gave me.

When I flew alone to Indiana for college at age 17, I spoke fluent Japanese.

Eight years later, I was a freelance Japanese-English translator when a tall bearded stranger chanced upon me at a Tokyo lunch table. It was Bradley Martin, bureau chief of The Wall Street Journal's Asian edition. He paid me to interpret at a Ministry of Finance interview — as a lark, he admitted later, to watch the bureaucrats' jaws drop at this American kid's Japanese. He soon gave me a part-time translating gig and, months later, forced me to report a story against my protestations that I had no journalistic talent.

I opened the newspaper, saw my byline, and had my Road to Damascus moment: This was my calling. Over the summer, Brad turned me into a journalist, a career richer than any I could have imagined.

I'm writing here because the sacrifices Dad made cued me up for Brad to take a gamble that guided me into my 38-year career and a life in which hundreds of people helped place me here in a blessed retirement.

Karen

"For the beauty of the earth, for the glory of the skies," we sang around the table at my 70th-birthday dinner last month in Kansas.

It was a hymn of thanks with special poignancy on this birthday. With me were three of my siblings, at the round table where we had gathered so many times with our parents, now long gone.

"For the love which from our birth, over and around us lies," we sang in four-part harmony, "Lord of all to thee we raise, this our hymn of grateful praise."

Steve and I have been singing fragments of that first verse to each other a lot this fall, even more often as Thanksgiving approaches and reminds us of the people in our lives that make our retirement more meaningful.

In San Francisco, that's church friends, former colleagues from schools where I taught, and friends we've made volunteering to develop a new park out by the beach. Retirement gives me more time simply to be with people here.

My 70th-birthday wish list had one entry: Gather with my brother and sisters and share stories. Around the Kansas farmstead table, we ate curry made with bison from a nearby preserve, I blew out a single candle on a birthday flan, and we retreated to the family room.

Each sibling and spouse showed an artifact about me from our past that prompted a story and a question for me — a photo of me in bell-bottoms in college, the first letter Steve wrote to me, before we were dating.

And then their gift of questions. What are your memories of the day we dropped you off for college in South Dakota? Which of your traits do you attribute to Mother? To Dad? As we age, we increasingly express gratitude for the values our parents instilled in us — unconditional love, creativity, an adventuresome spirit, generosity, willingness to let go.

Our three sons, whom we have long since let go, began phoning me that afternoon, giving me their good wishes.

My birthday celebration continued the next morning as we drove west across the Great Plains into the Colorado Rockies with the hymn of gratitude's first stanza in mind, "For the beauty of the earth."

Our retirement has deepened our gratitude for earth's beauty, at home in California, on our travels across America and in Japan. This birthday trip combined gratitude for both earth and family. We drove up an old mining road to the rustic cabin that Dad conceived and we helped build nearly 60 years ago with several other families and that has become a sacred place for our own children.

When we reached the cabin, out popped a birthday surprise: Our eldest son and our daughter-in-law had been lying in wait, bringing me another surge of gratitude.

Our hymn of gratefulness will accompany us again this month as we gaze out the windows of the eastbound Amtrak California Zephyr, absorbing America's beauty as we anticipate Thanksgiving week with our families in the Midwest.

With the tune running in our heads, we will give thanks "For the wonder of each hour, of the day and of the night, hill and vale and tree and flower.... For the joy of human love, brother, sister, parent, child, friends on earth, and friends above."

data.title: SA Asks: Should Nvidia bring back Jensen Huang?
data.description:
Should Nvidia bring back Jensen Huang as CEO?

We asked Seeking Alpha analysts Bashar Issa, Victor Dergunov, Danil Sereda, and The Techie for their thoughts.

Bashar Issa: Part of me wants Jensen Huang to stay out to break the “indispensable key person” myth used to justify billions in executive compensation, money that would otherwise go to investors who are actually taking the risk.

Moreover, as I mentioned in a recent article, Jensen Huang has been the hawk of the AI industry, pushing aggressive infrastructure buildout, adoption, and utilization by bringing all the players together. That control is one factor behind NVDA’s spectacularly high margins: for every $1 in COGS, Nvidia generates $4 in revenue.

That greed and opportunism aren't what the AI sector needs right now. High GPU costs are distorting data center unit economics, making everyone nervous, and creating market volatility. The sector needs a slowdown. The next phase is low margins and higher volumes to facilitate broader adoption, and Jensen Huang isn't the one to get us there.

Victor Dergunov: Jensen Huang is too much of a liability for Nvidia right now given the circumstances, and I don't envision him returning as CEO. It's possible he could come back in a more limited capacity, possibly as a consultant/executive, but ultimately, he would have much less control over the company and its future.

Danil Sereda: I think bringing back Jensen Huang right now would be a strategic and governance mistake, although tactically it would help Nvidia regain some of its lost billions in market cap in the short term.

As I addressed it in my recent article on Nvidia , Huang was an irreplaceable visionary founder, no questions about it. But Nvidia isn't a startup anymore that can be a one-man show, so to speak. He made a few mistakes, and the board accepted his resignation with no desire to reinstate him at this time. I think that's fair.

I also think that reinstating him would not make the intense federal scrutiny disappear. He is now expected to appear before House committees on Dec. 1 as an ex-CEO, not a current one. Given the questions that might be asked, if he returns before then, it could reignite regulatory chaos and undermine the credibility of the board.

Again, the board is probably the most important thing in a corporate structure, especially for a company with a multi-trillion-dollar market cap. Nvidia is likely to be fine because its operational engine didn't leave with its founder.

So, my short answer is no, Nvidia doesn't need to bring Jensen back. It can grow without him with the new, multi-role management structure in place.

(Danil Sereda leads the SA investing group Beyond the Wall Investing.)

The Techie: The board was too quick to take action on Jensen Huang’s resignation. To me, it’s very clear that Jensen should be brought back into the company, if not in the capacity of CEO, then in another position. That said, I don’t think we will see that happening, and I think that sooner or later the market must stop beating a dead horse.

The question to me now is who could replace him and how long that will take, because the company needs a clear leader to navigate everything happening, from anti-China laws to the custom ASIC threat.

data.title: Earnings Scoreboard: 11 of 14 reporting firms beat EPS estimates; 12 grow Y/Y profits
data.description:
Earnings season continues with 14 companies reporting quarterly results across communication services, consumer discretionary, consumer staples, and information technology.

Earnings Roundup:

Bottom Line: Out of the 14 companies reporting, 11 exceeded EPS expectations, while 3 came in-line. Notably, 12 firms posted year-over-year earnings growth.

Top Line: Out of the 14 companies reporting, 12 exceeded revenue expectations, while 2 fell below analyst estimates. Notably, all 14 firms posted year-over-year revenue growth.

Let’s take a look at some of the companies that reported earnings this week:

The Walt Disney Company : shares fell 1.48% post-earnings after beating Q4 estimates, with adjusted EPS of $1.77 (vs. $1.68 consensus) and revenue rising 16% Y/Y to $25.95B (vs. $25.2B est.). For FY27, Disney guided for double-digit adjusted EPS growth and ~8% segment operating income growth (ex-53rd week), while raising its annual dividend by 33% to $2.00/share.

The Home Depot : shares fell 2.45% post-earnings after beating Q3 estimates, with adjusted EPS of $3.86 (vs. $3.84 consensus) and revenue rising 4.9% Y/Y to $43.4B on 2.2% comparable sales growth. Management projected ~4.5% FY26 sales growth and 2.0% EPS growth, while naming CFO Richard McPhail to succeed Ted Decker as CEO effective November 23.

Lowe's Companies : shares rose 1.05% post-earnings after beating Q3 estimates, with non-GAAP EPS of $3.10 (vs. $2.90 consensus) and comparable sales rising 1.8% (vs. +0.4% est.) on a 17.4% jump in online sales. Management guided full-year sales to ~$92.5B (vs. $92.1B consensus) and adjusted EPS to $12.25 (vs. $12.27 est.), with comparable sales seen flat to +0.5%.

The TJX Companies : jumped 8.05% post-earnings after Q3 revenue rose 5.5% Y/Y to $15.95B on 4% comparable sales growth (beating the +3.8% consensus), while non-GAAP EPS of $1.34 matched estimates. Management guided full-year comp sales growth to 4% and EPS to $5.17–$5.20 (vs. $5.23 consensus), alongside plans to buy back ~$3.0B in stock during FY27.

Target Corporation : shares rose 4.01% post-earnings after a Q3 beat-and-raise, as tariff-refund tailwinds ($0.50/share) and <1% average ticket growth overshadowed 5.6% comparable sales growth (vs. 3.61% estimates) and adjusted EPS of $2.65 (vs. $2.08 estimates). Management raised FY26 guidance to ~6% sales growth ($111B) and adjusted EPS of $10.65–$11.40, while lifting capex to $5B–$6B.

Tyson Foods : jumped 8.72% post-earnings despite a 47% Y/Y drop in FQ4 adjusted EPS to $0.61 (vs. $0.62 consensus) as reported revenue rose 5.2% to $14.59B (-4.0% comparable). Deeper beef losses ($171M) and tighter chicken margins (8.7% vs. 12.7%) weighed on profits, while management projected FY27 sales to decline 3.5%–5.5% with $1.7B–$2.15B in adjusted operating income.

Walmart : slipped 1.04% post-earnings despite beating Q3 estimates, as a cautious holiday outlook tempered results. Adjusted EPS of $0.65 topped the $0.64 consensus, while U.S. comparable sales rose 2.9% (vs. 2.8% estimates) on a 23% jump in U.S. e-commerce; management guided FY27 revenue growth to 4.9%–5.2% and EPS to $2.84–$2.89 (midpoint $2.865 vs. $2.89 estimates).

Palo Alto Networks : surged 6.42% post-earnings after an FQ1 FY27 beat-and-raise, with adjusted EPS of $1.05 (vs. $0.97 consensus) and revenue rising 39% Y/Y to $3.45B (vs. $3.31B est.). Management raised FY27 revenue guidance to $14.52B–$14.57B and adjusted EPS to $4.26–$4.30 (vs. $4.18 estimates), alongside announcing a $4.5B all-stock deal to acquire Applied Compute.

NVIDIA Corporation : shares fell 2.89% post-earnings after delivering a strong Q3 beat-and-raise, reporting adjusted EPS of $2.68 (beating consensus by $0.21) and revenue surging 103.2% Y/Y to $115.84B ($7.13B above forecasts). Management guided Q4 revenue to ~$130B (±3%, vs. $124.89B estimates) and lifted FY28 revenue growth expectations to ~75% Y/Y, while noting it could exhaust its remaining $227.3B share buyback authorization by FY28.

Intuit : plunged ~12.8% post-earnings as soft guidance overshadowed a Q1 FY27 beat, with revenue up 12% Y/Y to $4.4B and non-GAAP EPS of $2.91 topping the $2.64 consensus. Amid Credit Karma softness, management guided Q2 revenue to $4.93B–$4.95B (vs. $5.11B estimates) and non-GAAP EPS to $3.17–$3.22 (vs. $3.94 estimates), while affirming FY27 non-GAAP EPS of $22.88–$23.12 (vs. $23.81 estimates). Intuit also agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons, acquired AI platform Sequence, and declared a $1.38/share quarterly dividend.

Keysight Technologies : shares fell 7.1% post-earnings after a Q4 beat-and-raise, with adjusted EPS of $3.61 (vs. $3.37 consensus) and revenue jumping 41% Y/Y to $1.99B (vs. $1.95B estimates). For Q1 FY27, management guided adjusted EPS to $3.63–$3.69 (vs. $3.21 estimates) and revenue to $2.04B–$2.06B (vs. $1.96B estimates).

data.title: IndusInd Bank Adds 4,300 Employees, Plans 100 Branches
data.description:
The lender is strengthening its frontline workforce and distribution network, with plans to open over 100 branches in the second half of FY27

IndusInd Bank has added approximately 4,300 employees across its operations, primarily in sourcing roles, as the private sector lender strengthens its frontline workforce and prepares to expand its branch network in the second half of the 2026-27 financial year.

The hiring expansion forms part of the bank's broader strategy to strengthen its sales and sourcing capabilities, improve market penetration and support business growth. The lender plans to open more than 100 branches during the second half of FY27, with a focus on underpenetrated markets and geographies where expansion had previously been limited.

Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Rajiv Anand outlined the workforce expansion during the bank's second-quarter earnings discussion on October 23, highlighting the importance of strengthening frontline capacity alongside its distribution network.

The bank is also accelerating the adoption of artificial intelligence across its operations. More than 50 per cent of its employees are using generative AI chatbots, with over half of these active users accessing the tools daily. The initiative is aimed at improving employee productivity and supporting routine business activities.

IndusInd Bank has additionally introduced six voice-bot programmes and identified 12 more customer and employee processes where conversational AI could be deployed. The bank is evaluating these applications to assess their potential operational benefits before expanding their use.

The simultaneous focus on workforce expansion and technology adoption reflects the lender's efforts to strengthen its physical presence while improving operational efficiency and customer engagement.

On the financial front, IndusInd Bank reported a net profit of Rs 1,242 crore in the second quarter of FY27, compared with a net loss of Rs 437 crore in the corresponding period of the previous financial year. The improvement was accompanied by stronger business momentum and better asset quality.

As of September 30, 2026, the bank operated 3,139 branches and banking outlets, supported by 2,773 ATMs. Its customer base stood at approximately 42 million.

The planned branch expansion and additional hiring indicate a renewed emphasis on frontline capacity and physical distribution as IndusInd Bank seeks to strengthen its presence in India's competitive banking sector.

data.title: XRP Price Could Have Its Worst Month in Recent History
data.description:
XRP has fallen below $0.90 for the first time in nearly two years, trading near $0.89. The token dropped more than 6% in 24 hours.

Now, with November losses topping 28%, XRP could close one of its worst months in recent history.

XRP Loses a Key Support for the First Time Since 2024

A support level is a price zone where buying demand has historically stopped a decline. For XRP, $0.90 had held on a sustained basis since November 2024.

That changed this week. The altcoin broke below the level amid a sharp deterioration across the crypto market. Bitcoin slipped below $56,000 and dragged most altcoins lower.

Just last week, XRP also posted its lowest weekly level for the first time in two years.

Meanwhile, US stocks suffered a heavy selloff, driven by weakness in tech and AI shares. Crypto liquidations also topped $1 billion in recent sessions, which amplified the selling pressure.

For XRP, the damage has been especially severe. The token now sits more than 75% below its record high near $3.65 from July 2025.

In November alone, XRP has lost over 28%. If the trend holds until month’s end, it could become the token’s worst month of the year.

It could also mark its weakest such month on record, surpassing the 23.6% drop seen in 2019.

How Much Lower Could XRP Go?

Bearish signals dominate for now. After losing $0.90, the next support sits near $0.80.

In a more pessimistic scenario, the token could slide toward the $0.64 to $0.70 zone.

Weak flows into spot XRP ETFs reinforce that outlook. According to SoSoValue, these funds have recorded about $30.8 million in net outflows in November.

That puts them on track for their worst month since launching in November 2025.

So far, March holds that record, with roughly $31.2 million in outflows. Meanwhile, total net assets have dropped below $1 billion to about $990 million, down from $1.42 billion in October.

As a result, buyers have struggled to defend key levels.

However, some indicators suggest XRP has entered extreme oversold territory. Bulls would first need to reclaim $0.90, which now acts as resistance.

After that, a recovery above $0.99 to $1.00 could open the path toward $1.10.

In a broader rebound, XRP could even revisit the $1.30 to $1.50 range. Historically, the token has staged strong recoveries after deep monthly losses, provided overall sentiment improves. Still, the altcoin has often struggled to rally while Bitcoin keeps falling.

For now, XRP sits at a critical point. The coming weeks should reveal whether $0.89 marks a temporary floor or the start of a deeper downtrend.

data.title: How a brutal week for stocks almost wiped out their gains for the entire year
data.description:
An earlier version of this article incorrectly included Costco's stock in Friday's selloff. It gained 0.8% and closed the week flat. By Joy Wiltermuth and Claudia Assis

Investors are now more focused on protecting their portfolios than looking for bargains

Fear on Wall Street is running high as the Nasdaq swings to a yearly loss and the Dow and S&P 500 give back most of their 2026 gains.

There wasn't much left of the stock market's earlier robust gains for 2026 after Friday's carnage.

Investors dumped artificial-intelligence beneficiaries Nvidia (NVDA), Sandisk (SNDK) and Micron (MU), alongside defensive areas like healthcare( )XX:SP500.303020, leaving few areas of the market unscathed ahead of the holiday-shortened Thanksgiving week.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA closed below the 50,000 threshold for a second straight day, joining the S&P 500 index SPX and Nasdaq Composite COMP in at least a 10% correction from their previous record closes.

Under the surface, things looked even more dire. A tally on Friday showed that 64% of the S&P 500's constituents closed at least 20% below their record highs, according to Dow Jones Market Data. That figure reached as high as 87% for the battered information-technology sector.

The S&P 500's information-technology sector has all but a sliver of its constituents down 20% or more from their record highs

"We are in the midst of a re-evaluation and a correction," said Jim Caron, chief investment officer of portfolio solutions at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Earnings and the economy still look good for next year, Caron said. But anxiety has only grown around the artificial-intelligence trade, especially with new scrutiny in Washington into sales of Nvidia's chips to China. There's also the U.S. midterm elections, which exposed how deeply unpopular the data-center boom has been with voters.

"It's not just about circular financing," Caron said, nor concerns about the speed of returns on AI investments. It's also a bigger conversation about how to build data centers in communities in a more sustainable and durable way. "We can't have a data center go in and everyone's electricity bill goes up," he added.

The hope was that Nvidia's stellar earnings and Anthropic's (ANT) historic IPO would staunch the bleeding this week in markets. And there was hope that investors might take heart in the economy's resilience and start picking through the stock-market carnage for bargains.

Instead, as of Friday the S&P 500 was up only 1% for the year, while the Dow was 0.2% higher and the Nasdaq was down 2.7%, according to FactSet.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 NDX was down 0.9% for the year, off more than 19% from its record high and on the cusp of a bear market.

Into the void

"It's a buyers' strike, even though we now have lower valuations," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services. There's also little clarity on what the next catalysts could be to shift sentiment back to a more positive direction, he said.

Stocks staged a dramatic rebound after President Donald Trump's April 9, 2025, pause on most of his reciprocal tariffs, as feverish dip-buying quickly erased the fallout in financial markets. The same pattern repeated several times during the first part of Trump's second term in the White House.

But with the "blue wave" soon putting control of the House and Senate in the hands of Democrats, Wall Street no longer expects an executive order or a social-media post that can shift market sentiment in an instant.

Is the AI punchbowl gone?

Investors have begun treating the midterm results as the moment the punchbowl was removed from the AI party.

"The midterms got rid of the assumption that there won't be pushback against data centers," said Keith Buchanan, a fund manager at Globalt Investments. "It made that part of it real."

As part of this, valuations in the stock market have come down dramatically. The S&P 500's information-technology sector was trading at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 16.3, based on Thursday's close, which was the lowest since the March 2020 COVID crisis, according to John Butters, a senior earnings analyst at FactSet. That's down from a 22 ratio at the beginning of 2026.

"This is almost like an epic rethink of the sector," said Truist's Lerner. "What it tells me is that people have lost confidence in the earnings outlook."

Wall Street now expects peak earnings growth this year, but for the S&P 500 to still see 16% to 17% earnings growth next year. But comments from Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller suggest the 2027 backdrop could be less business-friendly. He's been at the forefront in warning that a "shock" may be needed to coax inflation back down to the central bank's 2% annual target.

The Fed's next decision on rates is Dec. 9, with the odds favoring back-to-back rate hikes through January, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

Investors worry the Fed could tighten financial conditions too much and damage the economy.

The gloom hasn't improved even though global oil prices (BRN00) have tumbled almost 20% so far in November. Instead, Wall Street's "fear gauge" has surged more than 50% over the same stretch, with the below chart showing the Cboe Volatility Index VIX jump's above 30 on Friday.

When the "VIX" spikes, it implies there will be increased volatility in the S&P 500 over the next 30 days. That backdrop suggests investors might be more focused on protecting their portfolios, rather than looking to buy cheaper stocks.

As Caron at Morgan Stanley put it, "What's left over is the emotional aspect of preserving gains for the year."

data.title: Ashok Leyland truck plant to be set up in Singur, work to begin soon: Sukanta Majumdar
data.description:
Union Minister Sukanta Majumdar on Saturday said commercial vehicle manufacturer Ashok Leyland would set up a truck manufacturing plant in Singur, with work on the project expected to begin soon, reviving hopes of industrialisation at the site where the Tata Nano project was abandoned nearly two decades ago.

Speaking to reporters after Prime Minister Narendra Modi's programme at IIT Kharagpur, Majumdar said the BJP government was committed to bringing industry to Singur and that the proposed facility would manufacture heavy vehicles.

"We want to bring industry back to Singur. Our chief minister has also said so. I am reiterating today that Ashok Leyland is coming to Singur. It will set up a truck manufacturing plant, and work will begin soon," the Union minister of state for education said.

The announcement follows Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari's statement on November 5 that his government had held preliminary discussions with Ashok Leyland for setting up a heavy vehicle manufacturing unit in Singur.

Adhikari had then cautioned against making premature announcements, stressing that the government would prioritise projects capable of actual implementation over publicity-driven memorandums of understanding.

The latest announcement signals the BJP government's attempt to turn Singur, once synonymous with the collapse of a major industrial investment, into a showcase of its industrial revival agenda in West Bengal.

However, the project is yet to be formally detailed, with no investment outlay, employment projections or implementation timeline announced so far.

Majumdar also blamed successive state governments for Bengal missing out on major industrial opportunities, citing the semiconductor industry as an example.

"Taiwan is where it is today in the semiconductor industry, a position we could have occupied. The opportunity had come to us earlier, but the government of that time opposed computers, and consequently the semiconductor industry did not come up," he said, targeting the erstwhile Left Front government.

He also accused the Trinamool Congress government of failing to translate its industrialisation promises into concrete projects.

Singur's industrial future remains politically significant in Bengal, where the withdrawal of Tata Motors' Nano project in 2008 became a turning point in the state's politics.

The Left Front government, led by then Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee, had acquired around 997 acres for the proposed small-car factory.

A prolonged anti land acquisition agitation led by Mamata Banerjee, then the opposition leader, against the acquisition of farmland forced Tata Motors to abandon the project and shift it to Sanand in Gujarat.

The agitation helped propel Banerjee's Trinamool Congress to power in 2011, ending the Left Front's 34-year rule.

Her government subsequently returned the acquired land to unwilling farmers following a Supreme Court verdict, while the abandoned factory infrastructure was dismantled.

Nearly 18 years after the Nano project's exit, the proposed Ashok Leyland facility offers the BJP an opportunity to politically recast Singur as a symbol of industrial revival.

The project's credibility, however, will ultimately depend on translating the announcement into a concrete investment and a functioning manufacturing unit.

data.title: Titan looks to ramp up watch retail network to 500 stores
data.description:
Titan Company is looking to ramp up watch retail chain network to 500 stores by 2030 under Helios and Helios Luxe. This comes as the company has been strengthening its focus on premium and luxury watch segments. Also, the premium price points segments in the watch market are witnessing strong growth.

Rahul Shukla, Vice President and Chief Sales & Marketing Officer, Watches Division, Titan Company Ltd told businessline, “Every year we have been adding 30-40 stores. So at this pace of expansion, we would have close to 500 stores of Helios , out of which 40-50 will be Helios Luxe stores.”

On Friday, two new stores of Helios Luxe were launched in the Delhi-NCR region, taking the total count of the luxury watch boutiques to 16 across the country. Shukla said by the end of the year, the company expects to operating 25-30 Helios Luxe boutiques. Helios and Helios Luxe registered 35 per cent growth in the first half of the fiscal year.

Shukla pointed out that the watch market is witnessing strong growth in the segment priced above ₹25,000. “Helios and Helios Luxe are well-positioned to participate in this structural shift in the market, as evolving consumers are increasingly willing to uptrade, explore premium brands and seek differentiation. Helios and Helio Luxe are growing faster than category growth rates. Helios has been growing at 51 per cent and Helios Luxe has growning at 95 per cent,” he added.

While Helios stores offer products between ₹25,000 to about ₹1 lakh, Helios Luxe operates in the price point range of about ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh.

Shukla pointed out that Helios Luxe has also inked exclusive partnership with nine international brands over the last 24 months to build a strong portfolio. “With an expanding national footprint, a growing portfolio of distinctive watchmakers and a stronger focus on storytelling, Helios Luxe is looking to shape the next chapter of premium and luxury watch retail in India,” he noted.

data.title: Nvidia sinks roughly 40% as AI bubble fears drag Bitcoin below $60,000
data.description:
The AI trade is having its worst stretch yet. Nvidia shares have fallen roughly 40% in a matter of weeks, and the damage has spread well past Silicon Valley.

Bitcoin has slipped below $60,000. The total crypto market has contracted to approximately $2 trillion. When the poster child of a boom stumbles this hard, almost everything with a risk label feels it.

Nvidia closed at an all-time high of $243.37 on October 6, 2026. By mid-November, the stock was trading around $150.

That is a decline of about 40% from peak to trough. For a company that spent the past few years as the market's favorite growth story, the reversal has been swift.

The pain has not stayed confined to one ticker. The S&P 500 has entered correction territory, with weekly losses exceeding 8% as of November 21, 2026.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average has also slipped into a correction. Both benchmarks now sit more than 10% below their recent peaks.

At the center of the anxiety is a single question. Investors are asking whether the trillions of dollars flowing into AI infrastructure will ever earn back what they cost.

The numbers driving the worry are stark. AI infrastructure spending is projected at $7 trillion through 2030.

Gartner, the research firm, forecasts AI revenue over the same window at only $3.6 trillion. Put those two figures side by side and the gap is hard to ignore.

Nvidia sells the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush, mainly the chips that power data centers. If the companies buying those chips start doubting the payoff, they may slow their orders.

Bitcoin traded below $60,000 on November 21, 2026, with an intraday low somewhere between $55,000 and $57,000. The asset has now fallen more than 30% since September 2026.

The wider crypto market has fared no better. Total crypto market capitalization has shrunk to approximately $2 trillion, down from a peak above $4 trillion in October 2025.

The selling pressure on Bitcoin appears to reflect a broad, macro-driven liquidity squeeze rather than any problem specific to crypto. No major exchange failure or protocol exploit is behind this move.

Instead, Bitcoin is trading like what it has increasingly become: a high-beta risk asset that moves with tech stocks. When investors pull money out of speculative growth bets, digital assets tend to get swept up in the same tide.

The first takeaway is that the AI story and the crypto story are more tightly linked than many holders would like. A correction triggered by doubts over data center spending has knocked Bitcoin down by more than 30%.

Third, the gap between projected AI spending and forecast revenue is unlikely to close quickly. A $7 trillion capex bill against $3.6 trillion in expected revenue is a structural mismatch, not a quarterly blip. Each new earnings report from chipmakers and cloud providers will be read as evidence for or against the bubble thesis.

For crypto traders, the key signal may sit outside crypto entirely. As long as Bitcoin trades in step with the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, the path of the AI trade could help set the direction for digital assets too.

data.title: Lufthansa To Cut 1,000 Jobs At Flagship Airline
data.description:
Rising fuel costs, strike-related expenses and mounting losses have prompted the German airline to intensify its restructuring efforts

German airline Lufthansa plans to eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at its flagship airline, Lufthansa Airlines, as mounting financial pressures and rising operating costs force the company to accelerate its restructuring efforts.

The proposed job cuts will affect operations at the airline's Frankfurt and Munich hubs and represent approximately 2.5 per cent of its workforce of around 40,000 employees. The announcement was communicated to employees through an internal letter signed by Lufthansa Airlines chief executive Jens Ritter and other senior executives.

The management attributed the decision to the airline's deteriorating financial position, citing persistently high fuel prices, strike-related expenses and an already elevated cost base. The company said its earlier turnaround measures were no longer sufficient to secure its long-term financial stability.

During the first nine months of 2026, Lufthansa Airlines recorded an operating loss of approximately €180 million, translating into average monthly losses of around €20 million.

The internal communication also highlighted the impact of the conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to higher fuel costs, alongside nine days of strike action during the year. Management said these developments had further intensified the airline's operational and financial challenges.

The workforce reduction forms part of a broader efficiency drive that will also involve changes to the airline's flight operations and fleet strategy. Lufthansa plans to further reduce capacity on short and medium-haul routes and reduce the number of Airbus A320-family aircraft in its fleet, partially replacing them with smaller and more fuel-efficient Airbus A220 aircraft.

The airline is also accelerating the installation of Starlink satellite-based internet connectivity across its fleet, aiming to generate additional revenue through onboard connectivity services.

The latest announcement follows Lufthansa Group's September 2025 plan to eliminate approximately 4,000 administrative positions by 2030, primarily through digitalisation and the consolidation of administrative functions. However, it remains unclear whether the newly announced 1,000 job reductions at Lufthansa Airlines are included in that earlier target or represent additional cuts.

The restructuring comes amid wider challenges for the European aviation industry, particularly from volatile fuel prices, labour disputes and increasing pressure to improve operational efficiency. Lufthansa has also been engaged in negotiations with pilot unions over pay and working conditions, with disagreements continuing over proposed employment terms.

Interestingly, the financial performance of the wider Lufthansa Group has been relatively stronger than that of its flagship airline. The group reported a 30 per cent increase in net profit during the July-September quarter, supported by demand for premium long-haul travel. However, the core Lufthansa Airlines business continues to face profitability challenges.

At the end of 2025, Lufthansa Group employed 103,255 people worldwide, with approximately 64 per cent working across its passenger airlines. The latest restructuring highlights the distinction between the group's overall financial performance and the continuing pressure on its flagship carrier to improve productivity, control costs and restore profitability.

data.title: Broadcom AI outlook in focus beyond quarterly results, Goldman says
data.description:
For Broadcom , the focus would likely be beyond its quarterly results and on whether demand for AI chips can remain strong through 2028, as per Goldman Sachs analysts."We expect modest upside to guidance, but believe the stock will ultimately be driven more by clarity on the sustainability of AI spending into 2028, and Broadcom’s competitive position at key accounts such as Google," analysts at Goldman Sachs said.

AVGO stock was down 10% on Friday trading after a report revealed Google ()() is cutting planned shipments of its Broadcom-designed AI chips for 2027, while increasing orders for chips designed by MediaTek.

Concerns are growing about shortages of land, electricity, and buildings needed to house large-scale data centers. There are also questions about whether smaller cloud providers focused on AI will be able to secure enough outside funding to support their expansion. These emerging cloud providers account for about 6.3 gigawatts of Broadcom's planned 10 gigawatts of custom AI chip deployments in 2027. In 2028 emerging cloud providers are expected to account for about 75% of Broadcom's planned custom AI chip deployments.

Broadcom's competitive position is also at focus, especially after stock lost more than 10% value on Friday following reports of Google cutting Broadcom-designed AI chips while increasing orders for chips designed by MediaTek.

"We believe incremental detail on the durability of key customer engagements for next-generation XPUs as competitive intensity increases from providers such as MediaTek, could be impactful for the stock," Goldman analysts said.

Goldman cut the price target on Broadcom to $460 from $540, as it reduced the valuation multiple it applies to the company's expected earnings, from 30 times to 25 times.

Broadcom will report its fourth quarter results on December 9.

data.title: Bitcoin drops to lowest level in more than two years
data.description:
Bitcoin fell to its lowest level in more than two years late Friday as a widespread selloff in artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns over another Fed rate hike weighed on the ​world's largest cryptocurrency by market value.

Bitcoin’s selloff has coincided with a broader decline in the tech sector as investors review their investments in riskier assets amid fears over another Federal Reserve rate hike next month.

The abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO, and increasing regulatory risks for the cryptocurrency industry following the Democrats’ ​victory ⁠in the midterm elections have added another dimension to the bitcoin’s valuation debate.

“One explanation circulating in the market was that investors had been selling Bitcoin to free up capital for Anthropic's IPO,” wrote Seeking Alpha analyst BloFin Research. “However, Bitcoin has yet to see a meaningful rebound since the IPO, although one trading session is too early to determine whether such capital rotation will eventually occur,” the analyst added.

data.title: BlackRock's IBIT posts record $541M outflow as Bitcoin ETFs bleed $3.47B in November
data.description:
BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) just had the worst day in its history. On November 19, 2026, the fund recorded a net outflow of $541.1 million, its largest single-day redemption since launching in January 2024.

It wasn't an isolated bad afternoon, either. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have now shed approximately $3.47 billion in net outflows so far in November, and IBIT is doing most of the heavy lifting on the way out.

IBIT's $541.1 million exit topped its previous worst day: a $528.3 million outflow on January 30, 2026. That earlier record lasted less than a year.

Across all US spot Bitcoin ETFs, net outflows on November 19 totaled $582.3 million. That marked three consecutive days of redemptions for the group.

IBIT accounted for roughly 93% of that daily total. The concentration holds up over the full month too. BlackRock's fund represents about 85% of November's cumulative ETF outflows so far.

Other issuers felt the pressure, just on a smaller scale. Fidelity's FBTC lost $45.9 million on the day, while ARK 21Shares' ARKB saw $31.3 million leave.

One fund went the other way. Morgan Stanley's MSBT pulled in $49.6 million of fresh inflows on the same day, making it the rare product with money arriving rather than leaving.

The redemptions landed alongside a sharp slide in the underlying asset. Bitcoin traded around $61,800 to $62,000 on November 19, after falling below the $62,000 mark.

The price dropped about 3% over 24 hours and nearly 10% across the preceding week. That left Bitcoin at its weakest level since early July 2026.

The research behind this story ties the slide to macroeconomic pressure, including rising Treasury yields and shifting expectations around the Federal Reserve.

For all the red ink, the spot Bitcoin ETF complex remains large. The 12 US spot Bitcoin ETFs held approximately $76.6 billion in assets as of November 19.

That figure represents about 6.1% of Bitcoin's total market capitalization. Since their January 2024 debut, the funds have attracted around $53.5 billion in cumulative net inflows. Against that backdrop, approximately $3.47 billion in November outflows is a notable dent, though not a demolition.

The most striking detail is how concentrated the selling has been. When one fund accounts for roughly 93% of a day's outflows, the story is partly about Bitcoin and partly about who holds IBIT.

The MSBT inflow complicates any simple narrative of uniform panic. Some allocators were apparently still willing to add Bitcoin exposure on the same day others were trimming it.

For traders, ETF flow data has become one of the clearest windows into institutional and advisor-driven demand. Persistent outflows can add selling pressure to the spot market, since redemptions typically require funds to reduce their Bitcoin holdings.

data.title: Tentative Deal Averts Strike Threat at Busiest U.S. Ports — WSJ
data.description:
By Paul Berger

Port employers in Southern California and unionized security guards reached a tentative labor deal, averting a strike threat at the nation's busiest container-handling complex as retailers rush in last-minute holiday items.

The Pacific Maritime Association said early Saturday the current labor contract with 250 guards at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach would be extended pending ratification of the tentative deal by the workers.

The contract with the local chapter of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union had been due to expire at 12:01 a.m. Saturday and the guards had already voted to authorize a strike. Although the guards account for just 2% of the ports' unionized workforce, other ILWU dockworkers were expected to refuse to cross picket lines.

"This agreement provides certainty for the ports, for the cargo owners and workers throughout the supply chain who depend on them, and for the Southern California, regional and national economies," the employers said in a statement.

Union representatives didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Southern California ports have been deluged with cargo this fall. In October, the ports moved a combined more than 1 million loaded import boxes, measured in 20-foot-equivalent units, for the second month in a row as the traditional peak shipping season extended into the final quarter of the year.

Shipping industry officials had warned that a strike would affect six of the ports' 13 container-handling terminals, accounting for more than half of the gateway's cargo.

Port employers warned this week of growing potential for a strike because of a lack of progress in labor talks. The maritime association said earlier this week that its contract offer included a pay increase that would lift average full-time wages to $198,000 from more than $170,000.

The employers didn't provide details of the wage offer in the tentative deal.
